case.description: Create a reusable joint between two square rods in a tabletop pointer frame. The joint must let the operator exchange either rod while restoring the pointer's marked position without altering the rods.
case.valued_outcome: After five exchanges of each rod, the pointer returns within a 2 mm target circle and remains there during a supplied 10 N lateral load for ten seconds; each exchange takes less than forty seconds.
hard_constraints: No drilling, adhesive or permanent marks on either rod.
Joint envelope must fit inside a 90 mm cube.
Only hand-operated assembly and adjustment are permitted.
No component may fall free during an exchange.
resources: Two 400 mm square rods, measured sides 19 mm and 20 mm, plus one pointer and marked base.
Six plywood pieces each 80 by 40 by 6 mm, eight M5 bolts with nuts, four washers, two 150 mm elastic loops and 0.5 m of cord.
Hand drill for plywood only, saw, file, screwdriver and ruler.
One hundred minutes for fabrication and twenty minutes for testing.
observations: The current loose joint lets the pointer move 7 mm under the load.
Rod ends are square within the supplied 1 mm measurement resolution.
Awkward observation: the visually tighter rod fit returned 3 mm farther from the target after exchange than the looser fit in two supplied trials.

At most two joint configurations, twelve exchanges each and four load trials each.

openings.claim: Separate positioning from restraint: seat each rod against two fixed reference faces and an insertion stop before closing a captive clamp. This is a construction candidate, not demonstrated deployment.
openings.delta: Change the dependency from full-width tight fit to deliberate reference-face seating. Use plywood for the contact carrier, bolts for adjustment/stops, and cord or elastic keepers to retain moving pieces and fasteners. Accommodate 18, 19 and 20 mm rods through clamp travel rather than relocating reference faces.
openings.prediction: Nearest rival: tighter enclosure improves return accuracy through greater stiffness alone. The seating account predicts that a clearance configuration with consistent seating can return closer to the target than the tight configuration despite comparable loaded displacement. The rival predicts improved return and loaded displacement together as clearance decreases. Either pattern is uncertain; the two supplied trials establish neither cause.
openings.probe: Within the fabrication allowance, attempt one reference-seat assembly with two clearance settings. Before testing, check the complete joint fits a 90 mm cube, remains hand-operated, leaves rods unmarked, and retains every component throughout removal. Establish the marked pointer position once. For each setting, log five exchanges per original rod and two further exchanges using the 18 mm replacement, recording return position and elapsed seconds. Perform four ten-second 10 N trials, after exchanges 1, 5, 10 and 12. Compare return error and additional loaded displacement separately; retain the final two replacement observations as a distinct group. Keep both settings within twenty minutes total testing.
assumptions: Available plywood and eight bolts can provide sufficiently rigid reference faces, captive adjustment and insertion stops inside the envelope; detailed fastening geometry remains unresolved.
Defeat the candidate if references move, clearance prevents reliable seating, any component falls free, or fabrication/testing exceeds supplied capacity.
Reject operational adequacy if any required return/load exceeds the 2 mm circle or exchange takes forty seconds or more. A favorable comparison alone does not meet the valued outcome.

artifact.assessment: One opening retained. Seating-versus-stiffness discrimination is useful, but resource sufficiency and coupled effects limit interpretation. No reliability or load-capacity result is supplied.

openings.claim: A captive corner-datum joint may restore position more consistently if locating precedes clamping. The tighter-fit reversal could reflect premature frictional locking; this is unmeasured.
openings.delta: Change the locating dependency from overall tightness to two adjacent rod faces and an insertion stop. Use four plywood pieces as two fixed L nests and two as independently moving jaws; retain jaws, nuts and loops with cord. Seat each rod against its corner and stop before hand tightening. Lay out both nests inside the 90 mm cube; drill plywood only.
openings.prediction: Nearest rival: rod size or joint compliance dominates return error regardless of seating order. With equal final restraint, explicit seating should reduce exchange return error, including with the 18 mm replacement, without increasing loaded drift. Similar return distributions between orders would defeat the seating explanation; improved unloaded return with excessive loaded drift would defeat the proposed joint.
openings.probe: Fabricate one assembly and compare two operating configurations: explicit corner-and-stop seating before tightening versus tightening without that prescribed seating step. Allow twelve exchanges and four ten-second 10 N load trials per configuration. Exchange each original rod five times, then use the 18 mm replacement for the final two smaller-rod exchanges. Log time and unloaded/loaded target position. Both configurations must keep all components captive. Record deviations rather than asserting success.
assumptions: Bolt lengths and plywood attachment geometry must permit captive jaw travel within the cube; these dimensions are unspecified.
Available hardware must also provide stops and rigidly connect the nests; establish this from an actual layout before fabrication.
Plywood stiffness and hand tightening may be inadequate for the 2 mm loaded target.
Fabrication must finish within 100 minutes and comparisons within 20 minutes; actual capacity is unverified.

artifact.assessment: This is a bounded mechanism probe, not a deployment claim. Proceed only if the six-piece, eight-bolt layout physically supports separate captive locating and clamping. Failure to establish that layout makes the test infeasible; exchange caps alone do not resolve it.

openings.claim: Necessity hypothesis: restoring the pointer requires a close-fitting four-face enclosure matched to each rod. Neither tight fit implies the valued outcome nor the valued outcome implies tight fit is established; the awkward trials motivate removal, not a conclusion.
openings.delta: Remove dependence on rod-size-matched lateral fit. Construct two fixed two-face plywood datums with insertion stops, using plywood offcuts for pressure shoes. Hand-adjusted bolt pressure seats each rod against its datums while leaving clearance on the opposing faces. Keep bolts and nuts engaged during exchange; retain shoes with elastic loops and cord. The changed carrier is fixed contact geometry rather than an enclosing aperture.
openings.prediction: With unchanged datums and seating pressure, the clearance configuration can recover position across 19-to-18 mm substitution without refitting the aperture. Nearest rival: greater clamp restraint, rather than datum-based return, explains success. If both configurations return equally but only increased pressure improves loaded displacement, that rival gains support; if clearance improves unloaded return at comparable pressure while sustaining load, aperture removal gains support.
openings.probe: Fabrication probe only: within 100 minutes, build two settings of the same joint, ordinary close fit and opposing-face clearance, preserving datum positions. Verify the joint fits a 90 mm cube and every component remains attached throughout withdrawal. Use the ruler and fixed bolt-turn procedure to approximate comparable seating pressure; actual equality remains unknown. Within 20 testing minutes, conduct ten alternating exchanges per configuration: five of each rod, replacing the smaller rod with 18 mm for its last two exchanges. Log time and target return; perform four supplied 10 N, ten-second load trials per configuration. Reject if any exchange reaches forty seconds, return/load leaves the 2 mm circle, hardware detaches, or rods acquire permanent marks. Inability to fabricate captive shoes or finish measurements within resources defeats this probe; it does not establish necessity.
assumptions: Listed plywood and hardware permit sufficiently rigid, captive datums within the envelope.
Clamping can resist the supplied load without marking rods; capacity is unmeasured.

artifact.assessment: Source-compatible counterexample candidate with unresolved fabrication and restraint capacity; no demonstrated performance or deployment authorization.

openings.claim: The tighter fit may restrain motion while making exchange seating depend on friction or clamp-induced rocking. Replace that dependency with deliberate seating against fixed corner contacts and an end stop before hand-tightening each rod's captive closing bar.
openings.delta: Propose two independently releasable plywood seats joined inside the envelope. Use supplied bolts and nuts for closing bars and end stops; cord and elastic loops retain every released component. Nearest rival: clearance dominates both load displacement and exchange error, so a tighter surrounding fit should improve both.
openings.prediction: If seating history dominates, the corner-seated configuration should reduce unloaded return error despite allowing insertion clearance. If clearance dominates, the tight-fit configuration should have smaller loaded displacement without worse return error. These are competing predictions, not measured effects; the two supplied trials establish neither explanation.
openings.probe: Reuse the supplied materials for at most two configurations: corner seating followed by closure, and tighter surrounding contact. For each, log twelve exchanges: first five of each original rod, then the specified 18 mm substitution for the last two. Record target return and exchange time each time; conduct four ten-second 10 N trials after exchanges 5, 10, 11 and 12. Keep base and pointer attachment unchanged. Reject the candidate if return or loaded position leaves the 2 mm circle, any exchange reaches forty seconds, or retention fails. Fabrication exceeding 100 minutes or testing exceeding twenty defeats this probe's capacity; a time cap alone establishes no feasibility.
assumptions: Six plywood pieces and eight bolts can realize both seats, retention and stops within 90 mm; hardware lengths and frame geometry are unspecified.
Hand tightening supplies sufficient restraint without damaging rods; clamp force and friction are unknown.
Corner referencing can preserve the pointer datum after changing rod width; the 18 mm substitution can defeat this premise.

artifact.assessment: One discriminating opening. It preserves all requirements as acceptance conditions; fabrication, stiffness and substitution compatibility remain unproven. Probe only, with no deployment claim.
